event_subtitle: Exhibition Title: Diagrams of Memory: Interwoven Ontology
description:
Camille Ann Brewer lives and works in the City of Detroit, Michigan.  Through the process of textile construction, Brewer’s artwork intersects cartographic and photographic images that speak to specific spaces and time. Weaving together of physical place, memory with time is the core subject of this body of work.  

The artwork is built with time-period paper maps, which illustrate spatial geography and political territory; along with paper-collaged images of people, places and things, which tie directly to the history and human relationships in space.  In patterns that support the artwork’s theme, the two disparate paper elements are then woven together to create a serendipitous making and aesthetic experience.

combined_title: Comics Beyond Sight
description:
This exhibit covers a variety of creative approaches to comics visual accessibility, and by extension visual accessibility broadly. Those approaches range from multimedia (audio and textual descriptions) through multidimensional and emerging technologies strategies (3D printing, haptics, and screen-based mobile touch interfaces). It demonstrates that comics can be made accessible. Learn about the international efforts of innovators in the realm of comics accessibility for those who are blind or have low vision, assembled by the Accessible Comics Collective at San Francisco State University (SFSU) with the expertise of blind access professionals. 

Emily Beitiks was the accessibility lead for the content creation of the exhibit. She is the co-director for the San Francisco Disability Cultural Center (the first civically funded disability culture center on the planet!), and prior to that, the director of the Longmore Institute on Disability. 

Nick Sousanis (SFSU), the lead creative organizer of the exhibit, is a Detroit native and was the first person to draw his dissertation in comics format, subsequently published as the graphic novel Unflattening.

View the exhibit anytime the Hatcher Library is open, and join us for an opening presentation on Friday, October 2nd, 1:00pm - 4:00pm.

combined_title: Lila Kadaj Exhibition: Tic Tic
description:
Lila Kadaj received her MFA from Wayne State University. Her work has been shown at numerous institutions, including the Detroit Institute of Arts, the Cranbrook Art Museum, and the Arab American National Museum.  She spent nearly 27 years teaching art at Detroit Public schools.

Artist statement: “When looking at a beautiful flower.  It’s just itself.  Just there......no .....it does not proclaim its purpose for blooming is to make people happy. It just is. Like standing in front of an easel and painting........just is.......no matter......what proclamations may be concluded to sway the viewer. Same thing goes for fine art.  It’s not about I am a woman....it’s not about I am a first generation Arab American.....it’s not about being a child of trauma....it’s not about a member of my family being gunned down on the street....it’s about being born a painter.....standing in front of my easel and working to create a "Piece of Fine Art". Not standing on some soap box and expecting my words to somehow qualify my painting. It’s the painting, drawing or sculpture that must speak on its own.......on how the artist......via the intellect and muse uses the elements to create something distinct and first rate.   It can be quiet or loud. I see so much very weak work uplifted not for its quality but because it’s in fashion.”

event_title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
combined_title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
description:
Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union.

Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky  portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration.  

“For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.”
— Galina Lembersky, daughter

Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director.

Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky.

combined_title: Black Birth Joy: Announcing Lane Hall’s Fall Exhibition
description:
Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. 
 
Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. 

The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story.

The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan.

description:
Visit the Hatcher Gallery Exhibit Room to see historical materials that illustrate women’s changing relationship with food, cooking, and technology during the heady decade of the 1920s, sandwiched between WWI and the Great Depression. This exhibit features materials from the Janice Bluestein Longone Culinary Archive, as well as select items from the Art, Architecture, and Engineering Special Collections and the Transportation History Collection.

As America rang in a new decade in the 1920s, cookbook authors and appliance manufacturers stood ready to offer the newly emancipated and forward-thinking American woman a vision for her future, a vision that would be scientifically  grounded, speedy enough to make time for leisure as well as housework, and guaranteed to bring fun to that most humdrum of chores: planning and preparing meals for a family three times a day, 365 days a year.

combined_title: Like the flowing river: An exhibition by Tomoyuki Ueno
description:
Artist Tomoyuki Ueno creates individual works and installations where nature appears to be in an endless conversation with form, one echoing the other, a repetition. They are a combination of certainty and ephemerality, as if hinged between living and loss. The specificity of Ueno’s sculptural works reads like poetry. Ueno’s installation offers visitors time away, for contemplation, to draw inward, to come inside, to ask the question, “How are art and the everyday intertwined?” Honoring the Buddhist philosophy of impermanence, one becomes a continuation of the other. The artist intends the space to offer a restorative and meditative experience.

This exhibition includes artworks created from natural materials foraged by the artist while in artist residency in Ann Arbor.

*The title refers to the opening line of Hōjōki, written by 13th-century Japanese Buddhist monk Kamo no Chōmei: "The flow of the river is ceaseless, and the water is never the same…"*

Small Works
Prints & Book Objects from Detroit 2020–2026

October 27 - November 19 
Public Reception: Friday, November 13 from 4:30-6pm.

Small Works was a print shop ran by Li Chen & Gerald Schulze, in Detroit, MI, from 2020–2026. Mariana Matos joined as the studio assistant, and later studio manager, in 2024. Over those six years, the business grew from an extension of their design practice to a community space that hosts more than 70 classes a year, open studio for the public, and year long funded fellowships that investigate practice in art and design related to the Book Arts. In 2026, they decided to expand community programming, and to accommodate this expansion closed Small Works, and formed Center for the Book Arts Detroit (BAD) which operates in the same space.

This exhibition is a eulogy for the former Small Works shop, and a celebration of all the people who made work here. It also serves to show what is possible as a community, when they share space and create work together. 

The work featured is a collection of things printed by Small Works, by their studiomates Diskette Press, the publisher Maamoul Press, and by the community that uses the space.

event_title: The Emergence of Environmental Disparities: Evidence from a Century of U.S. Power Plant Openings
combined_title: The Emergence of Environmental Disparities: Evidence from a Century of U.S. Power Plant Openings: Danae Hernandez-Cortes, Arizona State University
description: This paper examines the emergence of Black-White disparities in exposure to air pollution from fossil-fuel power plants in the United States over the past century. We combine newly digitized data on annual power plant fuel consumption, emissions factors, and an atmospheric transport model to estimate county-level PM2.5 exposure over 1940-2020. We show that the exposure gap emerged in the 1950s, widened until 1980, and declined thereafter. To understand these patterns, we combine data on power plant openings (1900-2020) with U.S. Census demographics (1870-2020). We find little evidence that plants were disproportionately sited in counties with larger Black populations. Instead, event study estimates reveal that Black population shares increased by an average of 4 percentage points in the 50-70 years following a county's first plant opening. These shifts are concentrated in counties that first hosted a plant between 1900 and 1949 and reflect the contributions of the Great Migration, differential sorting in response to pollution, and other factors. Our findings highlight that the equity implications of siting long-lived infrastructure can differ dramatically depending on the time span considered.

event_title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
combined_title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism: Nicola Barham, Curator
description:
The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told.

*Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

description:
From September 2025 through December 2026, Stamps Gallery is partnering in a curatorial collaboration with two Southeast Michigan-based, artist-run project spaces led by Stamps alumni: C.Y.N.K. Studios, directed by Sally Clegg (Lecturer III and Student Exhibition Coordinator, MFA ’20) and Abhishek Narula (MFA ’20); and Sometimes Space, directed by Nathan Byrne (Lecturer I, MFA ’21). Each space hosts dozens of artists annually for exhibitions, performances, and events, fostering experimental work and building community. For this project, Byrne, Clegg, and Narula have been commissioned to reimagine the pillars on Division Street that flank the gallery. In response, they’ve curated six artists to create new work for the pillars over three cycles:

Phase 1 (September 12 - December 12) artists: Amelia Burns (Cranbrook MFA ’23) and Erin McKenna (MFA ’20)
Phase 2 (January 12 - August 12) artists: Sally Clegg (MFA ’20) and Kim Karlsrud (MFA ’20)
Phase 3 (September 11 - December 11) artists: Abhishek Narula (MFA ’20) and Nathan Byrne (MFA ’21)
Phase 3 

Curated by Sometimes Space: Abhishek Narula (entry pillar)
Curated by CYNK Studios: Nathan Byrne (courtyard pillar)

Artist Statements/Bios

Abhishek Narula, Compressions 
Compressions is an installation comprised of 416 industrial-grade zip ties, cinched around the entry pillar of the Stamps Gallery. The pillar measures roughly 110 inches in circumference, requiring two ties per row to wrap around it, resulting in 208 rows. The humble zip tie, typically used to hang and bind other material, is relegated to its functional properties rendering it unprepossessing and easily dismissed. The zip tie in this installation, instead serves as an object of aesthetic possibility, pulling it out of its usual background role to become the work itself. The resulting composition is a proposal to dwell, to slow down, and to simply see the pillar.

Abhishek Narula is an artist, designer, and educator who works across sculpture, installation, sound, and video. His practice takes the form of interventions, working with what is already present. He reorients and disrupts objects and sites in order to open up formal possibilities and poetic experiences within the familiar. He is influenced by physical and digital infrastructural systems that sustain modern life and culture. His work treats this ambience itself as raw material for aesthetic inquiry, exploring themes of labor, precarity, temporality and the sublime. Narula earned his MFA in Studio Art from the University of Michigan Stamps School of Art & Design and his MS/BS in Electrical Engineering from the Georgia Institute of Technology. His work has been exhibited at national and international venues such as the Ammerman Center for Arts and Technology, Science Gallery Detroit, Speculum Artium Media Festival in Slovenia, New Media Caucus (NMC), WaveFarm, The Boulder Public Library, The Hyde Park Art Center, Sector 2337 Art Gallery & Printing Press, Tangible Embedded Interaction (TEI), International Symposium of Electronic Arts (ISEA), among others. He is a Robotics Systems Designer and Lecturer in the Robotics Department at the University of Michigan. Website / Instagram

Nathan Byrne, Equally To Be Loved
Equally To Be Loved is an image / object scaled to and installed upon the courtyard pillar of Stamps Gallery. The image is of a spontaneous sculpture made in 2017 during the first day of an artist residency at the Recology San Francisco A.I.R. Program. The sculpture was constructed in a storage container studio using 14 discrete objects that were in his studio upon entry. For Byrne, this work embodies the energy and spirit of a studio at the start of a particularly fecund period of making. This work speaks to the artist’s interest in embodied experience of space, archival and site responsiveness, as well as his ongoing engagement with found materials. Byrne considers this project to be a far-flung sequel to his MFA thesis exhibition Equally Empty, which was shown at Stamps Gallery in 2021. Equally To Be Loved is the second line of the Buddhist mantra from which both titles are derived.

Nathan Byrne is an artist / educator / curator currently based in Detroit, MI. Through spatial and archive responsive projects, he reimagines, and explores within frameworks such as language, the passage of time, and contemplation. Intrigued by the potential of conveying phenomenal, transformative, and emotive states through materiality, process, and placement, he negotiates the pliability of the viewer’s encounters with objects and environments. Byrne holds an MFA in Art from the University of Michigan Stamps School of Art & Design and a BA in Studio Art and Art History from San Francisco State University. combined_title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
description:
Changes over the course of the nineteenth century in how Americans voted, from voice vote to public ballot box to private voting booth, also saw changes in the material culture that surrounded voting. Ballots and ballot boxes, campaign pins and ribbons, blank lists and pre-printed party tickets, lanterns and banners–the creative forces of the American print industry filled the country’s cities and small towns with the ephemera of electioneering.

As you look at the items in this exhibit, think about what they tell us about how Americans in the past felt about voting, and about how voting felt. How did Election Days feel when they were full of parades and music and public drinking? What was it like to vote when everyone around you knew who you voted for? And, most of all, who counted as a voter, and who did the counting?

Curated by Srimoyee Mitra

Stamps Gallery kicks off the fall 2026 semester with an ambitious mid-career survey of interdisciplinary artist Cosmo Whyte. Born and raised in Jamaica, Whyte completed a BFA from Bennington College and earned an MFA from the University of Michigan. He is currently a faculty member at the School of the Arts and Architecture, UCLA.

This exhibition brings together two central concerns that animate Whyte’s artistic practice: the archive, both personal and public, as a site of disturbance; and migration as a lived experience of refuge, refusal, and reinvention. In Whyte’s work, the archive is never static or neutral. Rather, it is a contested space where official histories encounter memory, inheritance, and the fragments of stories carried across generations. His practice moves within this charged interstitial terrain, between what has been recorded and what has been remembered, between institutional knowledge and embodied experience. Whyte invites the viewer to consider the fluidity of geographic borders and layered cultural identities that have persisted despite societal unrest caused by racial and socio-economic hierarchies across generations. In an era of intensified border politics and renewed debates over national identity, Whyte’s work offers a timely meditation on memory, movement, and belonging.

event_title: CREES Noon Lecture. Rehabilitative Postsocialism, Racialised Capital, and Yearning for Crip Horizon
combined_title: CREES Noon Lecture. Rehabilitative Postsocialism, Racialised Capital, and Yearning for Crip Horizon: Kateřina Kolářová, associate professor of sociology, Charles University, Prague
event_subtitle: Kateřina Kolářová, associate professor of sociology, Charles University, Prague
description:
Drawing on her new book, *Rehabilitative Postsocialism: Disability, Sex, and Race in Eastern Europe*, Kateřina Kolářová will argue that postsocialism is essential to understanding neoliberal cultural politics, economic structures, and state policies worldwide. She will show how disability, sexuality, and race—though often rendered invisible—have shaped the postsocialist consensus in the Czech Republic and more broadly.

The talk will focus on how discourses of “inadaptability” have contributed to racialized abandonment. Kolářová will examine how particular understandings of disability helped establish an ideal of rehabilitated, white postsocialist citizenship. She will also consider the “neoliberalization of race” and the “racialization of neoliberalism” (Mahtani and Roberts) within the specific historical and political context of the Czech Republic and post socialist Eastern Europe. Specifically, Kolářová will explore how portrayals of Roma people as “inadaptable (non)citizens” have been used to determine who belongs in shared public spaces and whose exposure to violence is treated as morally defensible. The talk will conclude by examining forms of resistance that open up alternative possibilities, or “crip horizons.”

Kateřina Kolářová is associate professor of sociology at Charles University in Prague. Kolářová’s other recent work takes the feminist queer crip perspective to explore the bio-social dimensions of metabolism, “crip guts,” the relationship between human and non-human lives, and how we coexist with microorganisms, toxic chemicals, and other "unclean" elements/entities. She is currently working on a monograph exploring HIV and human-viral coexistence (forthcoming in 2027). She is a passionate forager, fermentation enthusiast, and an avid chaos gardener.

Her book *Rehabilitative Postsocialism: Disability, Sex, and Race in Eastern Europe* (University of Michigan Press, 2025) is available on "Open Access." It was the winner of the 2019 Tobin Siebers Prize for Disability Studies in the Humanities.

Open Access link to book: https://www.fulcrum.org/concern/monographs/xd07gw749

event_title: HET Brown Bag Seminar |  Long-range interaction between extremal black holes in two derivative effective theories of gravity
combined_title: HET Brown Bag Seminar |  Long-range interaction between extremal black holes in two derivative effective theories of gravity: Aritra Saha (Texas A&M)
description: In two derivative theories of gravity, the long-range force between a generic extremal black hole and its identical copy vanishes. On the other hand, if extremal black holes are supersymmetric, then the long-range force (and short-range as well) between any two such black holes vanishes. This brings up the interesting question of what happens to the long-range force between two extremal black holes when they are generically non-supersymmetric? In this talk, we will develop a framework for two derivative theories of gravity coupled to scalars and gauge fields which will generically allow us to estimate the long-range force between two non-identical black holes without knowing their explicit metrics. We shall discuss this framework first in the context of Einstein-Maxwell-Dilaton theory in 4D with a single arbitrary coupling constant (called "a''), and extend this discussion to higher dimensions. We shall see that the long-range force shows a universal feature: the force vanishes for the supersymmetric coupling (a=1), it remains repulsive if the coupling is tuned to be greater than the supersymmetric coupling (a>1), and it becomes attractive if the coupling becomes less than the supersymmetric coupling (a<1). We shall then add axions to the discussion and show how the universality of the long-range force becomes more murky. Finally we shall develop an understanding of the long-range force using the interaction energy picture within the initial value formulation of gravity, owing to Brill and Lindquist.

event_title: NCKS Colloquium Series | Dying Tree: Embodying Jungyong in Contemporary Korean Choreography
combined_title: NCKS Colloquium Series | Dying Tree: Embodying Jungyong in Contemporary Korean Choreography: Jae-duk Kim: Choreographer, Composer, and Artistic Director
event_subtitle: Jae-duk Kim: Choreographer, Composer, and Artistic Director
description:
Synopsis:
Dying Tree is an original movement practice developed by choreographer Kim Jaeduk through improvisation and close observation of the body. Inspired by his reflections on Jungyong (中庸), a philosophical concept rooted in Confucian thought, this practice explores how movement can be sustained and transformed aesthetically through the interplay of force and balance, speed and expression.

This colloquium takes as its starting point an image that emerged from observing Kim Jaeduk's improvisational movement: a body that appears almost motionless, like a dying tree in winter, while an intense flow of energy continues within. This contrast between outward stillness and inner vitality connects to a longstanding question in Kim Jaeduk's choreographic practice: how can movement be sustained through continuous change? The image became a point of departure for developing the physical principles of Dying Tree and gradually shaping them into a distinct movement style.

The presentation explores how the concept of Jungyong is embodied through several key movement principles. These include Chumi (醜美), which explores asymmetrical bodily forms and the aesthetic potential of unconventional shapes; Jwause (左右勢), which organizes lateral shifts and changes in the body's center; and Changyeong (贊輕), which cultivates a deliberately light quality of movement.
The presentation also examines the relationship between Hyeongsik(形式), the structural organization of movement that can be physically learned and repeated, and Hyeongyong (形容), which expands its expressive possibilities. Through this relationship, it considers how established movement structures can become the basis for new choreographic expressions.

Combining a spoken presentation with live movement demonstrations, the colloquium shows how philosophical ideas can inform physical exploration, movement training, and the creative process of contemporary choreography.

Rather than presenting Dying Tree as a direct representation of a particular philosophical tradition, this colloquium approaches it as an ongoing artistic practice through which ideas are interpreted, tested, and explored through the body. From Kim Jaeduk's choreographic perspective, it seeks to illuminate how embodied knowledge, philosophical inquiry, and creative experimentation intersect in the making of contemporary dance.

Biography:
Kim Jae-duk is an internationally acclaimed South Korean choreographer and composer, currently serving as the Artistic Director of Modern Table Contemporary Dance Company in Korea and Resident Choreographer of T.H.E Dance Company in Singapore.

Recognized for his distinctive choreographic language, Kim creates dynamic works that bring together contemporary dance, music, rhythm, and physical expression. His artistic practice explores the relationship between movement and sound, drawing inspiration from diverse cultural influences and traditional rhythmic structures to develop a unique and powerful performance vocabulary.

Kim has established an extensive international presence through commissions and collaborations with leading dance companies across Asia, Europe, Oceania, and South America. His choreographic works have been presented by institutions including the Argentine National Contemporary Dance Company, Lucerne Municipal Dance Company TanzLuzern in Switzerland, Hong Kong City Contemporary Dance Company (CCDC), New Zealand Dance Company, Curitiba Municipal Ballet in Brazil, and the Seoul Metropolitan Dance Theatre.

His notable works include Tension Espacial, commissioned by the Argentine National Contemporary Dance Company in 2015 and subsequently revived for a total of 48 performances in 2026; Jangdan, created for Hong Kong CCDC; Brown, which received three awards at the 2023 Hong Kong Dance Awards; JE-UI, commissioned by TanzLuzern; and MEDITA, which received the 2025 Grand Prize in Choreography from the Korean Association of Dance Critics. His work Sokdowas also selected for the official showcase of Tanzmesse in Germany in 2020.

In recognition of his outstanding artistic achievements, Kim received the 2024 New York Bessie Award for Outstanding Choreography. His other accolades include the Korea Modern Dance Association's Choreographer of the Year Award, three awards at the 24th Hong Kong Dance Awards in 2023 for Brown, the Music & Sound Design Award at the 21st Hong Kong Dance Awards in 2019 for Jangdan, and a Commendation from the Minister of Culture, Sports and Tourism of Korea in 2018.

Beyond his choreographic work, Kim is actively involved in international artistic exchange and education. He has led workshops and participated in residency and educational programmes at major international platforms, including ImPulsTanz – Vienna International Dance Festival and the Centre National de la Danse (CND) in Paris. In 2008, he was invited to lecture at the Rambert School of Ballet and Contemporary Dance in the United Kingdom.

Through his ongoing work in Korea and Singapore, as well as his collaborations with international dance companies and cultural institutions, Kim Jae-duk continues to expand the possibilities of contemporary dance, establishing a distinctive artistic voice on the global stage.

combined_title: The Tree of Eternity: Interactive arttech exhibit
description:
The Tree of Eternity is an immersive, interactive installation that explores remembrance, loss, and the enduring presence of those we have loved. 

The installation centers on a projected tree surrounded by interactive terminal pods that control its structure.

Visitors approach interactive pods positioned throughout the gallery space, where they are invited to recall memories of people or experiences throughout their lives. Depending on the kiosk they interact with, different effects will be present on the projected tree.

As more visitors’ memories are inputted, the tree’s visuals adapt and change form, demonstrating that our memories persist with us. Projection mapping creates ethereal visuals accompanied by atmospheric audio. Even when visitors aren't actively engaging with the kiosks, the system generates ambient transmissions, suggesting that the tree—and the memories it embodies—continues to live and grow.

The installation creates a dialogue between life and death, presence and absence, individual memory and collective remembrance, inviting participants to contribute to a living memorial that persists beyond any single moment of grief or reflection.

event_title: Interdisciplinary QC-CM Seminar | Topological defects in quantum materials: what the spectrum, the S-matrix and the STM tip know
combined_title: Interdisciplinary QC-CM Seminar | Topological defects in quantum materials: what the spectrum, the S-matrix and the STM tip know: Eric Akkermans (Technion)
description: Point defects in chiral or particle–hole-symmetric crystals are topological objects: a vacancy in graphene binds a zero mode fixed by an index theorem, carrying a quantized, measurable charge. I will show how this topology is encoded in three places an experiment can reach:  the displaced-state count, the scattering matrix, and the local density of states, and how an exact closed formula for the defect's scattering determinant yields a sum rule that distinguishes a true vacancy from a strong impurity. The same index structure governs interacting electrons bound to several defects, where the Coulomb interaction entangles the protected modes, and extends, unexpectedly, to the topological classification of two-qubit gates.

Featured Scholar: Preeti Varma, INSEAD

Description: In an ethnographic study of employees at Multivex (MV), an AI development company building frontier multimodal AI models, I present a theoretical model describing the social construction of aspirational intoxication, defined as a state of captivation with an imagined future. I find that workers confront a tension arising from the simultaneous promise and threat of advanced AI to society’s future—a tension amplified by accelerating technological capabilities and nested competitive races. This tension generates an intractable anxiety (moral, existential, and competitive) about the future. Rather than avoiding or accepting this anxiety, workers engage in three cognitive processes—intellectualizing narratives, abstracting identity, and gamifying reality—that transform anxiety into fascination, significance, and thrill. This study helps explain how workers become increasingly invested in realizing transformative technological futures, and how such investment reinforces the competitive dynamics that accelerate their development and sustain technological progress.

event_subtitle: Jessica Pan, National University of Singapore
description: Gender gaps in promotion remain widespread and are accounted for, at least in part, by gender differences in promotion desire. We study the role of managers in shaping the gender gap in promotion desire. Using detailed personnel data from the second largest property insurance company in Japan, we leverage plausibly exogenous manager rotations to estimate each manager's effect on the promotion desire of the female employees they supervise. Event studies validate these estimates: moving to a manager with a higher estimated fixed effect raises women's promotion desire, with no corresponding effect for men. The effects appear to operate through supportive, development-oriented management; managers less conducive to women's promotion desire tend to prioritize business outcomes over people development and impose longer hours in their teams.

description:
Abstract: 
The Psyche spacecraft was launched on October 23, 2023 from Kennedy Space Center on a Falcon Heavy Rocket. The launch began the spacecraft’s 2.2 billion mile journey to the asteroid 16 Psyche in the outer part of the main asteroid belt between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter. The Psyche asteroid, composed of over 50% metal by weight is possibly the metal core of a planetesimal whose formation was interrupted early in the solar system by collisions with other bodies that created the asteroid belt. The Psyche spacecraft is a hybrid. Maxar/Intuitive-Machines, now known for taking photographs from space over Ukraine, fabricated the spacecraft bus based on heritage hardware, and JPL installed scientific payload, avionics and autonomous flight software for deep space operation. This $900M NASA mission is the first spacecraft to use Hall thrusters in deep space to rendezvous and orbit the asteroid, and recently completed a Mars Gravity Assist on the way to rendezvous in 2029. A 2-year science program will determine the asteroid’s composition and remnant magnetic field to determine if this unique object really is a planetary core…and what that actually looks like. The talk will describe the Psyche mission and provides updates on electric propulsion at JPL.

About the Speaker: 
Dr. Dan M. Goebel received a B.S. in physics in 1977, an M.S. in EE in 1978, and a Ph.D. in applied plasma physics in 1981 from UCLA. He is a Fellow and Senior Research Scientist at JPL and an Adjunct Professor of Aerospace Engineering at UCLA. At JPL he is the Chief Engineer of the Psyche Mission and responsible for the development of advanced spacecraft technologies. Dr. Goebel is a member of the National Academy of Engineering, the National Academy of Inventors, and Fellow of the AIAA, IEEE, and APS. He is the author of over 300 technical and conference papers, two textbooks on Electric Propulsion, and holds 60 patents.

event_title: A New Approach for the Continuous Time Kyle-Back Strategic Insider Equilibrium Problem
combined_title: A New Approach for the Continuous Time Kyle-Back Strategic Insider Equilibrium Problem: Bixing Qiao, UM
description:
In this talk, we consider a continuous-time Kyle-Back model which is a game between an insider and a market maker. The existing literature typically focuses on constructing equilibria with a PDE approach, which requires certain Markovian structures. We characterize all equilibria through a coupled system of forward-backward SDEs. In particular, when the time duration is small, we show that the FBSDE is well-posed, and therefore the game has a unique equilibrium. Moreover, this unique equilibrium may be non-Markovian and thus not attainable via the PDE approach. We next study the set value of the game, which roughly speaking is the set of insider's values over all equilibria and thus is by nature unique. Finally, we characterize the set value through a level set of a certain standard HJB equation.
In the second part of the talk, we apply the new approach to the Kyle-Back model with dynamic legal risk and large numbers of noise traders. In this setting, the insider chooses a strategy that conceals his identity within a large volume of surrounding trades and concentrates on medium-sized trades.  We establish an intensity-based mathematical framework for explaining the interconnections between insider trading and stealth trading. When the number of noise traders becomes large, the price impact of the insider asymptotically vanishes, and consequently the stochastic game becomes deterministic optimizations, which also carry implications for regulatory investigations and sanctions.

The results above include the joint work with Weixuan Xia and with Jianfeng Zhang.

event_subtitle: "Digital tissue twins: turning histology into spatial omics at population scale"
description:
Abstract: Spatial omics technologies are reshaping how we study the molecular organization of tissues, offering unprecedented opportunities to map biology in its native spatial context. However, key challenges remain in resolution, scalability, and accessibility. In this talk, I will describe how my lab is developing Al-powered approaches that integrate spatial omics with histopathology to overcome these barriers. I will highlight computational strategies that make spatial omics experiments smarter, faster, and more informative, from enhancing spatial resolution beyond current experimental limits, to extending analyses across large and complex tissues, to integrating diverse molecular measurements within a unified framework. Together, these approaches enable the creation of "digital tissue twins," computational representations of tissues that capture both molecular and structural organization. Finally, I will discuss our efforts to design Al systems that are transparent and trustworthy, ensuring that these tools can support robust biological discovery and clinical translation. These advances aim to unlock the full potential of spatial omics and enable new insights in the era of precision medicine.

Bio: Dr. Mingyao Li joined the Biostatistics faculty in 2006. She is also a faculty member of the Genomics and Computational Biology graduate program. Her main research area is statistical genetics and genomics. The central theme of her current research is to use statistical and machine learning approaches to understand cellular heterogeneity in human disease relevant tissues, to characterize gene expression diversity across cell types, and to study the patterns of cell state transition and crosstalk of various cells using data generated from single-cell transcriptomics studies. In addition to methods development, Dr. Li is also interested in collaborating with researchers seeking to identify complex disease susceptibility genes. Her collaborative research includes cardiometabolic diseases, age-related macular degeneration, Alzheimer's disease, chronic kidney disease, type 1 diabetes, and cancer. Findings from her research will seed cell-specific functional studies, in vivo modeling, and precision therapeutic targeting of human diseases. Dr. Li actively serves in the scientific community. She is an Associate Editor of Statistics in Biosciences, and was a regular member of the Genomics, Computational Biology and Technology study section and a member of the review committee of the Center for Inherited Disease Research of the NIH.

event_title: RTG GEOMETRY, TOPOLOGY, DYNAMICS    On isomorphism classes of (topological) Lefschetz pencils on ruled surfaces
combined_title: RTG GEOMETRY, TOPOLOGY, DYNAMICS    On isomorphism classes of (topological) Lefschetz pencils on ruled surfaces: Carlos Servan
description: Lefschetz pencils, originally discovered by Lefschetz in the context of algebraic varieties, were later shown to be intimately related to symplectic manifolds by work of Donaldson and Gompf. In fact, we have a correspondence: Every symplectic 4-manifold admits a Lefschetz pencil and the total space of every such pencil is symplectic. Nonetheless, this correspondence is not canonical. A natural question is then the following: Given a fixed symplectic manifold, does it admit more than one (inequivalent) Lefschetz pencil of fixed genus? How about infinitely many? In this talk we will discuss these questions in the context of Ruled surfaces. In particular, we will show that for any ruled surface of negative euler characteristic the answer to both questions is Yes. This is joint work with Seraphina Lee.

description:
U-M College of Pharmacy Pharmaceutical Sciences John G. Wagner Pharmacia & Upjohn Memorial Lecture Series

Speaker: Dr. Mark Slifka, Ph.D.,
Professor, Oregon Health & Science University

Title: Vaccine Durability – what have we learned so far?

Abstract: In this presentation, I will begin by discussing the importance of maintaining high vaccination coverage in the face of vaccine skepticism and science denialism. Next, I will examine various models on how long-term vaccine-induced antibody responses are maintained including the role of memory B cells, long-lived plasma cells, TLR agonist adjuvants, and the role of antigen structure and an antigenic threshold in determining the duration of immunological memory. The presentation will end with an analysis of immunity following tetanus/diphtheria vaccination, in which I propose that we may no longer need to recommend booster vaccinations for adults once they have completed their full childhood vaccination series. This modest change to the U.S. vaccination schedule could save up to $1 billion annually without reducing the protection afforded by these two important legacy vaccines.

description: Engendering Respectful Communities (ERC) is a one session workshop that engages graduate students in meaningful dialogue about various forms of sexual misconduct they may encounter in both professional and social spaces, and provides resources for intervention or support in such circumstances.The primary goal of the workshop is to address complexities experienced by graduate students as they engage in bystander intervention, so that participants gain an increase in awareness of barriers to action and familiarity with strategic planning to overcome them. The workshop also introduces participants to on-campus resources and provides knowledge on how sexual misconduct can unfold in graduate-specific settings.The ERC workshop uses small-group circles intended to promote active reflection and space to build community. The procedure of circles is introduced at the beginning of the workshop in order to help participants get used to the process, which they do through a circle for introductions and value-sharing for the workshop space. These circles depict various, realistic scenarios related to sexual misconduct within the graduate community. The circle process allows circle members to process the monologues, reflect on complexities with identity and power dynamics within them, name potential barriers to intervention, and think of various ways in which they might respond if faced with similar situations. The circles provide a way to foster collective building of ideas, where participants learn from one another and all input is equally valued. Participants are encouraged to share but can always pass if desired, creating an environment where participation is open but not forced. Due to the participatory nature of the workshop, if you are to arrive more than 20 minutes late, we will ask you to re-register for another workshop session.If you have any questions about or concerns with taking this workshop, or are in need of an exemption, please contact jhippe@umich.edu or fill out this form. We know some students come to campus having already experienced harm. If you have circumstances that make completing this course challenging, please reach out to the GROWE team. SAPAC GROWE provides exemptions to the ERC workshop (where requirements are set in place) on a case by case basis. The Program Manager will communicate with students requesting exemptions via email and/or meet with students via zoom meetings to discuss their need for exemptions and provide any relevant and necessary resources.

description:
Fungi are familiar to most of us. Mushrooms pop up in our yards after a rainstorm. Yeast brew our beer. Maybe you’ve foraged for morels or picked up a sourdough hobby. If you think you know fungi, though, think again! Just this summer a team of U-M researchers discovered an entire world of fungi thriving nearly a third of a mile underground, including 13 new species that have never been described before.

Jack Tucker is hilariously awful, and that’s precisely the point.

The Jack Tucker Comedy Standup Show is the misguided brainchild of Zach Zucker, a performer who is celebrated for blending virtuosic clowning with razor-sharp satire. His character Jack Tucker is a well-respected journeyman and bonafide legend on the Upstate New York regional comedy scene, a catastrophically overconfident stand-up comedian whose hacky punchlines, misplaced swagger, and desperate need to be adored convince him that he’s going to make it big any day now.

As his jokes collapse and his bravado frays, the show exposes the fragile ego beneath the spotlight and the quiet terror behind the mic. Equal parts parody, performance art, and masterclass in comedic tension, Jack Tucker Comedy Standup Show walks a thrilling line, with Zach Zucker’s physical control and improvisational daring bringing both discipline and danger to the chaos.

Zucker, whose clown lineage dates to the famous École Philippe Gaulier in France, the training ground for actors such as Sacha Baron Cohen, Helena Bonham Carter, Emma Thompson, and many others, is a cult favorite on the international comedy circuit, known for his always sold-out Stamptown Comedy and a forthcoming Netflix special.

Lila Kadaj received her MFA from Wayne State University. Her work has been shown at numerous institutions, including the Detroit Institute of Arts, the Cranbrook Art Museum, and the Arab American National Museum.  She spent nearly 27 years teaching art at Detroit Public schools.

Artist statement: “When looking at a beautiful flower.  It’s just itself.  Just there......no .....it does not proclaim its purpose for blooming is to make people happy. It just is. Like standing in front of an easel and painting........just is.......no matter......what proclamations may be concluded to sway the viewer. Same thing goes for fine art.  It’s not about I am a woman....it’s not about I am a first generation Arab American.....it’s not about being a child of trauma....it’s not about a member of my family being gunned down on the street....it’s about being born a painter.....standing in front of my easel and working to create a "Piece of Fine Art". Not standing on some soap box and expecting my words to somehow qualify my painting. It’s the painting, drawing or sculpture that must speak on its own.......on how the artist......via the intellect and muse uses the elements to create something distinct and first rate.   It can be quiet or loud. I see so much very weak work uplifted not for its quality but because it’s in fashion.”

event_title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
combined_title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
description:
Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union.

Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky  portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration.  

“For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.”
— Galina Lembersky, daughter

Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director.

Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky.

combined_title: Black Birth Joy: Announcing Lane Hall’s Fall Exhibition
description:
Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. 
 
Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. 

The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story.

The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan.

description:
Artist Tomoyuki Ueno creates individual works and installations where nature appears to be in an endless conversation with form, one echoing the other, a repetition. They are a combination of certainty and ephemerality, as if hinged between living and loss. The specificity of Ueno’s sculptural works reads like poetry. Ueno’s installation offers visitors time away, for contemplation, to draw inward, to come inside, to ask the question, “How are art and the everyday intertwined?” Honoring the Buddhist philosophy of impermanence, one becomes a continuation of the other. The artist intends the space to offer a restorative and meditative experience.

This exhibition includes artworks created from natural materials foraged by the artist while in artist residency in Ann Arbor.

*The title refers to the opening line of Hōjōki, written by 13th-century Japanese Buddhist monk Kamo no Chōmei: "The flow of the river is ceaseless, and the water is never the same…"*

Small Works was a print shop ran by Li Chen & Gerald Schulze, in Detroit, MI, from 2020–2026. Mariana Matos joined as the studio assistant, and later studio manager, in 2024. Over those six years, the business grew from an extension of their design practice to a community space that hosts more than 70 classes a year, open studio for the public, and year long funded fellowships that investigate practice in art and design related to the Book Arts. In 2026, they decided to expand community programming, and to accommodate this expansion closed Small Works, and formed Center for the Book Arts Detroit (BAD) which operates in the same space.

This exhibition is a eulogy for the former Small Works shop, and a celebration of all the people who made work here. It also serves to show what is possible as a community, when they share space and create work together. 

The work featured is a collection of things printed by Small Works, by their studiomates Diskette Press, the publisher Maamoul Press, and by the community that uses the space.

event_title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
combined_title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism: Nicola Barham, Curator
description:
The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told.

*Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

combined_title: Fore-Site (Phase 3): The Stamps Gallery Pillar Project
description:
From September 2025 through December 2026, Stamps Gallery is partnering in a curatorial collaboration with two Southeast Michigan-based, artist-run project spaces led by Stamps alumni: C.Y.N.K. Studios, directed by Sally Clegg (Lecturer III and Student Exhibition Coordinator, MFA ’20) and Abhishek Narula (MFA ’20); and Sometimes Space, directed by Nathan Byrne (Lecturer I, MFA ’21). Each space hosts dozens of artists annually for exhibitions, performances, and events, fostering experimental work and building community. For this project, Byrne, Clegg, and Narula have been commissioned to reimagine the pillars on Division Street that flank the gallery. In response, they’ve curated six artists to create new work for the pillars over three cycles:

Phase 1 (September 12 - December 12) artists: Amelia Burns (Cranbrook MFA ’23) and Erin McKenna (MFA ’20)
Phase 2 (January 12 - August 12) artists: Sally Clegg (MFA ’20) and Kim Karlsrud (MFA ’20)
Phase 3 (September 11 - December 11) artists: Abhishek Narula (MFA ’20) and Nathan Byrne (MFA ’21)
Phase 3 

Curated by Sometimes Space: Abhishek Narula (entry pillar)
Curated by CYNK Studios: Nathan Byrne (courtyard pillar)

Artist Statements/Bios

Abhishek Narula, Compressions 
Compressions is an installation comprised of 416 industrial-grade zip ties, cinched around the entry pillar of the Stamps Gallery. The pillar measures roughly 110 inches in circumference, requiring two ties per row to wrap around it, resulting in 208 rows. The humble zip tie, typically used to hang and bind other material, is relegated to its functional properties rendering it unprepossessing and easily dismissed. The zip tie in this installation, instead serves as an object of aesthetic possibility, pulling it out of its usual background role to become the work itself. The resulting composition is a proposal to dwell, to slow down, and to simply see the pillar.

Abhishek Narula is an artist, designer, and educator who works across sculpture, installation, sound, and video. His practice takes the form of interventions, working with what is already present. He reorients and disrupts objects and sites in order to open up formal possibilities and poetic experiences within the familiar. He is influenced by physical and digital infrastructural systems that sustain modern life and culture. His work treats this ambience itself as raw material for aesthetic inquiry, exploring themes of labor, precarity, temporality and the sublime. Narula earned his MFA in Studio Art from the University of Michigan Stamps School of Art & Design and his MS/BS in Electrical Engineering from the Georgia Institute of Technology. His work has been exhibited at national and international venues such as the Ammerman Center for Arts and Technology, Science Gallery Detroit, Speculum Artium Media Festival in Slovenia, New Media Caucus (NMC), WaveFarm, The Boulder Public Library, The Hyde Park Art Center, Sector 2337 Art Gallery & Printing Press, Tangible Embedded Interaction (TEI), International Symposium of Electronic Arts (ISEA), among others. He is a Robotics Systems Designer and Lecturer in the Robotics Department at the University of Michigan. Website / Instagram

Nathan Byrne, Equally To Be Loved
Equally To Be Loved is an image / object scaled to and installed upon the courtyard pillar of Stamps Gallery. The image is of a spontaneous sculpture made in 2017 during the first day of an artist residency at the Recology San Francisco A.I.R. Program. The sculpture was constructed in a storage container studio using 14 discrete objects that were in his studio upon entry. For Byrne, this work embodies the energy and spirit of a studio at the start of a particularly fecund period of making. This work speaks to the artist’s interest in embodied experience of space, archival and site responsiveness, as well as his ongoing engagement with found materials. Byrne considers this project to be a far-flung sequel to his MFA thesis exhibition Equally Empty, which was shown at Stamps Gallery in 2021. Equally To Be Loved is the second line of the Buddhist mantra from which both titles are derived.

Nathan Byrne is an artist / educator / curator currently based in Detroit, MI. Through spatial and archive responsive projects, he reimagines, and explores within frameworks such as language, the passage of time, and contemplation. Intrigued by the potential of conveying phenomenal, transformative, and emotive states through materiality, process, and placement, he negotiates the pliability of the viewer’s encounters with objects and environments. Byrne holds an MFA in Art from the University of Michigan Stamps School of Art & Design and a BA in Studio Art and Art History from San Francisco State University. He has been a Lecturer at Stamps School of Art & Design since the Fall of 2022. His work is exhibited widely nationally and he is a recipient of the VSC Fellowship at Vermont Studio Center. He has been awarded numerous artist residencies including Anderson Ranch Arts Center, I-Park, KHN Center for the Arts, Prairie Ronde, Recology San Francisco A.I.R. Program, and Rockland Woods. event_title: Quantum Research Institute | Emerging Rare-Earth-Alloyed III-Nitrides for Quantum Photonics and Advanced Electronics
combined_title: Quantum Research Institute | Emerging Rare-Earth-Alloyed III-Nitrides for Quantum Photonics and Advanced Electronics: Jiangnan Liu (University of Michigan)
description:
Zoom: In the Meeting Invite

In-Person: Michigan Memorial Phoenix Project, 2301 Bonisteel Blvd, Ann Arbor, MI 48109, USA, PML 2000

Abstract:
Group III-nitride semiconductors have enabled a broad range of applications from solid-state
lighting to high-power electronics. Alloying III-nitrides with rare-earth elements such as Sc, Y,
and La offers new pathways to tailor their fundamental optical and electronic properties, with
substantial enhancements in piezoelectricity, ferroelectricity, and second-order optical
nonlinearity (χ (2) ). These emerging materials offer a multifunctional platform for integrated
quantum photonics and advanced electronics.
In this talk, I will discuss the molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) growth and comprehensive
characterization of several rare-earth-alloyed III-nitrides, focusing on the effects of alloying on
second-order optical nonlinearity and its role in enabling ferroelectric polarization switching. I
will then discuss the opportunities to develop new device concepts for both photonic and
electronic applications through heterostructure engineering. Specifically, I will present an ultra-
low-loss hybrid ScAlN/SiNₓ integrated photonic platform for quantum photonics, followed by
electronic device demonstrations in which ferroelectric ScAlN barriers are integrated into
conventional high-electron-mobility transistors (HEMTs). These devices achieve record-low
sheet resistance, fast operation speed, and exceptional thermal stability.

Bio:
Jiangnan Liu is a postdoctoral research fellow at the University of Michigan, where he also
earned his Ph.D. in Electrical and Computer Engineering. His research focuses on the molecular
beam epitaxy (MBE) growth and device integration of emerging ferroelectric III-nitride
semiconductors for the next-generation photonic and electronic applications.

event_title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
combined_title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
description:
Changes over the course of the nineteenth century in how Americans voted, from voice vote to public ballot box to private voting booth, also saw changes in the material culture that surrounded voting. Ballots and ballot boxes, campaign pins and ribbons, blank lists and pre-printed party tickets, lanterns and banners–the creative forces of the American print industry filled the country’s cities and small towns with the ephemera of electioneering.

As you look at the items in this exhibit, think about what they tell us about how Americans in the past felt about voting, and about how voting felt. How did Election Days feel when they were full of parades and music and public drinking? What was it like to vote when everyone around you knew who you voted for? And, most of all, who counted as a voter, and who did the counting?

On view September 11-December 22, weekdays from 12-4 pm.

Thirty-minute recitals are performed on the Charles Baird Carillon at noon every weekday that classes are in session, followed by visitor Q&A with the carillonist. Take the elevator to the highest floor possible (floor 8), and then climb two flights of stairs (39 steps) to the bell chamber (floor 10). Hearing protection earmuffs are provided for visitors. Be prepared to walk on ice and snow in the bell chamber during winter. Built in 1936, the Charles Baird Carillon is not ADA accessible. event_title: Cosmo Whyte: Under the Quiet, Beyond the Eye
combined_title: Cosmo Whyte: Under the Quiet, Beyond the Eye
description:
Curated by Srimoyee Mitra

Stamps Gallery kicks off the fall 2026 semester with an ambitious mid-career survey of interdisciplinary artist Cosmo Whyte. Born and raised in Jamaica, Whyte completed a BFA from Bennington College and earned an MFA from the University of Michigan. He is currently a faculty member at the School of the Arts and Architecture, UCLA.

This exhibition brings together two central concerns that animate Whyte’s artistic practice: the archive, both personal and public, as a site of disturbance; and migration as a lived experience of refuge, refusal, and reinvention. In Whyte’s work, the archive is never static or neutral. Rather, it is a contested space where official histories encounter memory, inheritance, and the fragments of stories carried across generations. His practice moves within this charged interstitial terrain, between what has been recorded and what has been remembered, between institutional knowledge and embodied experience. Whyte invites the viewer to consider the fluidity of geographic borders and layered cultural identities that have persisted despite societal unrest caused by racial and socio-economic hierarchies across generations. In an era of intensified border politics and renewed debates over national identity, Whyte’s work offers a timely meditation on memory, movement, and belonging.

Presented with support from the U-M Institute for Humanities, the U-M LSA Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies, and the U-M Library.

event_title: Missing Results of Discrimination: A Meta-Analysis of Racial, Gender, and Intersectional Discrimination Using Correspondence Audits
combined_title: Missing Results of Discrimination: A Meta-Analysis of Racial, Gender, and Intersectional Discrimination Using Correspondence Audits: S. Michael Gaddis, Georgia State University
event_subtitle: S. Michael Gaddis, Georgia State University
description:
CID Speaker Series

Join the Stone Center for Inequality Dynamics as we host S. Michael Gaddis, clinical associate professor of management and policy in Georgia State University’s Andrew Young School of Policy Studies.

Abstract: Intersectionality theory argues that race and gender cannot be fully understood in isolation or through an additive approach. This study introduces a systematically comparative framework for identifying missing results in correspondence audits and helping scholars conduct more holistic analyses. Drawing on 52 correspondence audits encompassing nearly 330,000 tests, it identifies patterns that can be missed when racial and gender discrimination are analyzed separately rather than through an intersectional framework, and offers best-practice recommendations for designing, analyzing, and citing correspondence audits.

Gaddis is a methodologist with expertise in survey and experimental design whose research advances understanding of inequality and discrimination across multiple dimensions.

combined_title: The Tree of Eternity: Interactive arttech exhibit
description:
The Tree of Eternity is an immersive, interactive installation that explores remembrance, loss, and the enduring presence of those we have loved. 

The installation centers on a projected tree surrounded by interactive terminal pods that control its structure.

Visitors approach interactive pods positioned throughout the gallery space, where they are invited to recall memories of people or experiences throughout their lives. Depending on the kiosk they interact with, different effects will be present on the projected tree.

As more visitors’ memories are inputted, the tree’s visuals adapt and change form, demonstrating that our memories persist with us. Projection mapping creates ethereal visuals accompanied by atmospheric audio. Even when visitors aren't actively engaging with the kiosks, the system generates ambient transmissions, suggesting that the tree—and the memories it embodies—continues to live and grow.

The installation creates a dialogue between life and death, presence and absence, individual memory and collective remembrance, inviting participants to contribute to a living memorial that persists beyond any single moment of grief or reflection.

combined_title: ChE SEMINAR: Mark Tuckerman, New York University: Crystal Math: Rapid and accurate prediction of molecular crystal structures and properties using topological and simple physical descriptors, informatics, and generative models
event_subtitle: Crystal Math: Rapid and accurate prediction of molecular crystal structures and properties using topological and simple physical descriptors, informatics, and generative models
description:
Abstract: 
The different solid structures or polymorphs of atomic and molecular crystals often possess
different physical and chemical properties. Structural differences between organic molecular
crystal polymorphs can affect, for example, bioavailability of active pharmaceutical formulations,
the lethality of contact insecticides, the performance of molecular electronic devices, and diffusive
behavior in host-guest systems. Such differences can also influence the behavior of smart materials, such as self-healing crystals. Crystallization conditions can influence polymorph selection, making an experimentally driven hunt for polymorphs difficult. Theory and computation can potentially play a vital role in mapping the landscape of crystal polymorphism. Traditional methods for predicting crystal structures and investigating solid-solid phase transformation behavior face their own challenges, and therefore, new approaches are needed. In this talk, I will show, by leveraging concepts from mathematics, specifically geometry and topology, in combination with simple physical principles, database processing that we have been able to develop a new framework, which we are calling “CrystalMath” that represents a new paradigm in our ability to predict molecular crystal structures and crystal properties, orders of magnitude faster and with far fewer resources than more traditional methods. Examples to be presented will show that CrystalMath can handle molecules with considerable flexibility by decomposing them into rigid fragments and applying the rules of CrystalMath to them separately and rejoining the molecules after application of the rules. In our series of examples, we will resolve a long-standing controversy concerning the polymorph landscape of the anti-cancer drug Galunisertib and show how to predict crystal structures of molecules as complex as ritonavir. I will also discuss the challenges associated with generative AImodels and describe how it can be tuned to have some impact on the problem while pushing for the use of AI in more downstream tasks such as property prediction.

Acknowledgements. This work was supported by the National Science Foundation grant nos.
CHE-1955381 and DMR-2118890 as well as grants from Pfizer Inc. and Abbvie Inc.


Bio: 
Mark Tuckerman is a native of California who obtained his B.S. in physics from the University
of California at Berkeley in 1986 and his Ph.D. from Columbia University in 1993, working in
the group of Bruce J. Berne. From 1993-1994, he held an IBM postdoctoral fellowship at the
IBM Forschungslaboratorium in Rüschlikon, Switzerland in the computational physics group of
Michele Parrinello. From 1995-1996, he held an NSF postdoctoral fellowship in Advanced
Scientific Computing at the University of Pennsylvania in the group of Michael L. Klein. He is
currently Professor of Chemistry, Physics, and Mathematics at New York University. His
research program spans a variety of topics including development of free-energy based enhanced
sampling tools for predicting the conformational equilibria of complex molecules, development
of novel methods for predicting structure and polymorphism in molecular crystals, simulation
studies of electrolyte liquids for clean energy applications, development of machine learning
models for electronic structure theory and statistical mechanics applications, and path-integral
methods for quantum dynamics. Honors and awards include the Japan Society for the
Promotion of Science Fellowship, the Friedrich Wilhelm Bessel Research Award from the
Alexander von Humboldt Foundation, the Camille Dreyfus Teacher-Scholar Award, an NSF
CAREER Award, and the NYU Golden Dozen Teaching Excellence Award, the Andreas C.
Albrecht Lectureship from Cornell University, the Pitzer Lectureship from UC Berkeley, the
Kennedy Lectureship from Washington University, the Institute Lectureship from the Indian
Institute of Technology, Kanpur, where he was selected as Distinguished Visiting Professor,
election as a Fellow of the AAAS, a Dreyfus award for Machine Learning in the Chemical
Sciences and Engineering, an Einstein Fellowship from the Einstein Stiftung Berlin, a CNRS
Fellowship, the Linett Professorship from the University of Cambridge, and recent award of
Doctor Honoris Causa from the Université de Toulouse. He is the Principal Investigator and
Director Elect of the Simons Center for Computational Physical Chemistry at New York
University and former Chair of the Department of Chemistry at NYU.

event_subtitle: "Making Learning Visible: Reflection, GenAI, and Measurement in Authentic Learning Environments," with Alexandra Werth, Ph.D.
description:
Making Learning Visible: Reflection, GenAI, and Measurement in Authentic Learning Environments
Abstract:
Authentic learning environments, such as capstone design or undergraduate research experiences, give engineering students opportunities to practice being an engineer. These learning environments are often characterized by students needing to navigate uncertainty, exercise judgment, and learn through collaboration. Yet measuring this learning is challenging, particularly across engineering’s diverse educational contexts. Students’ written reflections offer both a way to support learning and a window into how they make sense of their experiences. How can we use these rich, traditionally qualitative accounts to investigate patterns in learning across students and settings?

Our research addresses four connected challenges: eliciting substantive reflection, establishing what students’ accounts can tell us about the learning we value, interpreting those accounts reliably, and producing findings that can inform educational practice. This seminar focuses on developing methods and tools that elicit deeper student reflection and support reliable analysis, drawing on both pedagogical design and new capabilities of generative AI.

I will share work exploring AI-personalized short-form reflections and longer reflective memos, alongside human and AI-assisted approaches to analyzing students’ writing. These examples bring questions of validation, interrater reliability, and the role of course context into focus. Together, they contribute to a broader effort to develop measurement approaches that preserve the richness of students’ experiences while supporting research across learning environments and helping instructors improve their own courses.    
Bio:
Alexandra Werth is an assistant professor in Cornell University’s Meinig School of Biomedical Engineering and a core faculty member of the Duffield Engineering Education Research Institute. She directs the Biomedical Engineering Education, Assessment, and Research (BEEAR) Lab, where her group studies how students learn and develop as engineers through research, design, and other authentic learning experiences. Her work examines reflection, feedback, and teamwork while developing human and generative AI-assisted methods for studying learning across educational contexts. She leads NSF-funded projects on AI-augmented reflection and pedagogical practices for engineering teamwork and received Cornell Engineering’s 2025 EPICC Award for Innovation.

Werth holds bachelor’s degrees in engineering and physics from Swarthmore College and a Ph.D. in Electrical and Computer Engineering from Princeton University, where her research focused on noninvasive glucose sensing using quantum cascade laser spectroscopy. She subsequently conducted postdoctoral research in physics education at the University of Colorado Boulder, studying undergraduate laboratory learning and helping developed the first large-enrollment introductory physics course-based undergraduate research experience.

combined_title: IOE 899: Jim Dai, Cornell University: "A Framework for Scalable Control of Stochastic Processing Networks"
event_subtitle: "A Framework for Scalable Control of Stochastic Processing Networks"
description: Stochastic processing networks (SPNs) model the operations of many complex systems, such as data centers and communication networks. These networks have been an active subject of research for more than 40 years. In this talk, Dai will introduce M-COF (Multi-scale Closed-form Optimization Framework), a new framework for the optimal control of a class of SPNs known as multi-class queueing networks. M-COF is scalable, can incorporate practical performance metrics such as tail-latency or fairness, and is rooted in recently developed multi-scale heavy-traffic theory. He will also discuss the relationship between M-COF (simulation-free) and recent methods (with simulation) based on deep PDEs and deep reinforcement learning. This talk is based on joint work with Jin Guang (Chicago Booth) and Lucy Huo (HKUST).
