event_title: IES Energy Seminar Series - AI-Based Analytics and Energy Modeling Frameworks for Characterizing Urban Energy Systems
combined_title: IES Energy Seminar Series - AI-Based Analytics and Energy Modeling Frameworks for Characterizing Urban Energy Systems: Rawad El Kontar, NLR
description:
Abstract: 
Urban energy systems are growing in complexity as they respond to the challenges of planning location-specific energy transitions. However, current modeling approaches often fail to capture the physical, behavioral, and systemic diversity required for effective localized planning and decision-making.

In this talk, I will present integrated frameworks that combine bottom-up physics-based modeling with AI-driven analytics for characterizing urban energy systems. I will first show how the URBANopt platform has developed capabilities that enable coordinated analysis and co-design across buildings, DERs, and the grid. I will then discuss an AI-driven capabilities that automates input generation and supports dynamic scenario exploration.

These capabilities transform urban energy system planning by reducing the labor required for model generation, scaling scenario exploration, and improving accuracy for localized analysis. Together, they form a scalable and adaptable framework that provides stakeholders with actionable insights for planning reliable and efficient energy transitions.

Biography:
Dr. Rawad El Kontar is a Senior Research Engineer at the U.S. Department of Energy’s National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR). He is the lead developer of URBANopt, DOE’s open-source urban energy modeling platform, and the creator of the Urban Systems Generator, an AI-driven framework that automates building-level data completion and scenario generation for city-scale energy modeling. With a multidisciplinary background spanning architecture, building science, and data science, Rawad develops analytics and software platforms that integrate machine learning, AI, and energy simulation to accelerate the co-design and optimization of buildings, distributed energy resources (DERs), and grid systems. His work supports stakeholders in advancing reliable and efficient energy.

event_title: The Astrophysics of Quasars Probed using Broad Absorption Line Quasars
combined_title: The Astrophysics of Quasars Probed using Broad Absorption Line Quasars: Dr. Karen Leighly
description:
All massive galaxies host a supermassive black hole at their centers. Sufficient gas falling onto the
black hole creates a quasar that is dramatically brighter than its host galaxy; in fact, quasars are the
most luminous persistently emitting objects in the Universe. While the infalling gas powers the
quasar, the light it emits can, in turn, power an outflow that can be observed in the rest-frame UV
spectra. However, despite more than 50 years of study, the physical properties of quasar winds,
including fundamentals like the location of the outflow and the wind's potential for influencing
galaxy evolution, are largely unmeasured.

We pioneered the novel spectral synthesis software SimBAL, which uses forward modeling and a
Bayesian calibration to extract the physical conditions of the BALQ wind. Using SimBAL, we are
learning about the properties of winds, and the demographics of the winds is revealing aspects of the
quasar central engine. In this talk, I will highlight what we have learned, and describe some of our
future investigations.

event_title: Beyond Local Revenue: Commercial Property Taxes, Firm Behavior, and Fiscal Externalities
combined_title: Beyond Local Revenue: Commercial Property Taxes, Firm Behavior, and Fiscal Externalities: Nathan Sunday, University of Michigan
description: Property taxation is widely viewed as a promising source of revenue for developing countries, yet evidence on its economic effects remains limited. Using administrative data from corporate and employee tax returns in a staggered difference-in-differences design, this paper shows that a property tax increase in Kampala, Uganda significantly reduced rates of firm survival. Business rental expenses increased by 6.3 percent, and firms responded by reducing formal employment and wages, with wage informalization accounting for most of the decline in the formal wage bill. Higher-earning employees of ongoing firms bore disproportionate shares of the wage declines. Within government, there were vertical fiscal externalities: the tax increase reduced central government income tax revenues by 30 percent of the amount it contributed to local property tax collections.  The estimates imply that property taxes have 53 percent marginal deadweight losses.

event_title: Colloquium: Introduction to the Kakeya Conjectures
combined_title: Colloquium: Introduction to the Kakeya Conjectures: Ruixiang Zhang, University of California, Berkeley
event_subtitle: Ruixiang Zhang, University of California, Berkeley
description:
The Kakeya Conjectures concern overlapping properties of direction-separated tubes in $\mathbb{R}^n$. They are elementary to state, but difficult to prove. In 2025, Wang-Zahl proved the Kakeya Set Conjecture for n=3. On October 6, OpenAI claimed progress on Kakeya Conjectures in dimensions 3 and 4. Then on October 26, OpenAI claimed to have resolved these conjectures in all dimensions by proving Sogge's Local Smoothing Conjecture for free waves. 

I will introduce the Kakeya Conjectures and various human attempts, showing its many faces and why some approaches appeared difficult. I will also discuss how the Kakeya Conjectures connect to harmonic analysis and which directions mathematicians hoped a complete solution would unlock. Then I will share some first impressions on OpenAI's proposed proof for the Local Smoothing Conjecture on October 26.

event_title: Cutting Through Time: Folk Heritage and Socialist Vision in Chinese Papercuts
combined_title: Cutting Through Time: Folk Heritage and Socialist Vision in Chinese Papercuts: Third Thursdays at the Library
description:
Deeply woven into the fabric of daily life, Chinese papercuts (jiǎnzhǐ 剪紙) have long marked domestic spaces and life-cycle rituals. This exhibit showcases the rich tapestry of regional styles, distinct cutting techniques, and enduring motifs preserved across generations. Drawn from several significant donations to the Asia Library, alongside our rich print collection on Chinese paper arts, we'll highlight both rare original artworks and publications that provide context for them.

Beyond traditional themes, our collections also reveal how papercutting transformed into a medium of political and social mobilization throughout the twentieth century. In the 1940s, artists at the revolutionary base in Yan’an adapted local paper arts to convey socialist ideals. Following the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949, more and more art schools, local workshops, and professional artists were involved in the creation of papercuts, depicting collective labor, communist ideology, and industrial progress. During the Cultural Revolution (1966-1976), new papercuts largely illustrated political campaigns and eulogized party leaders. By the reform era of the 1980s, papercuts entered global markets as exported handicrafts and cultural ambassadors, marking yet another reinvention of a timeless folk tradition.

In 2009, Chinese papercutting was inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, honoring centuries of technical virtuosity and communal creativity across China’s diverse regions and ethnic groups.

event_title: FAST Lecture | The Site of the Horti Sallustiani in Rome
combined_title: FAST Lecture | The Site of the Horti Sallustiani in Rome: Francesca Zandonai, Freie Universität Berlin
description:
Join us at this month’s FAST Lecture to hear from Francesca Zandonai, a junior visiting scholar from Freie Universität Berlin.

The objective of Francesca’s doctoral research project is to investigate the topographical and architectural evolution of the Horti Sallustiani site in Rome and to develop a new understanding of how this multifunctional garden complex evolved—a key aspect that has received little attention in scholarship to date. By employing digital methods, her project will provide a digital, diachronic topography of all archaeological finds and features discovered within the area of the Horti Sallustiani. This will allow for a critical re-evaluation of the existence and function of the garden complex. As a starting point for this topographical inquiry, Francesca will examine both historical excavations and more recent, unpublished archaeological investigations.

FAST (Field Archaeology Series on Thursday) Lectures are free and open to the public. The talk will take place in Room 125 of the Kelsey Museum’s Newberry Hall. Light refreshments will be provided at 5:30 PM, with the lecture starting at 6:00 PM.

description:
Jorge M. Pérez is a collector, philanthropist, and the founder of El Espacio 23, a contemporary art space in Miami that presents exhibitions, residencies, and special projects drawn from the Pérez Collection. Housed in a repurposed 28,000-square-foot warehouse in the city’s Allapattah neighborhood, El Espacio 23 reflects Pérez’s commitment to supporting artists, fostering curatorial practice, and expanding public access to contemporary art.

As the Founding Executive Chairman of Related Group, Pérez has helped shape South Florida’s urban landscape for more than four decades. A lifelong advocate for the arts, he has championed the integration of museum-quality contemporary art into the built environment while building one of the country’s leading private collections. His philanthropic support includes a landmark gift that led to the naming of Pérez Art Museum Miami (PAMM), where he has continued to contribute both funding and works from his collection.

Pérez and Related Group have partnered with world-class architects and designers like Arquitectónica, Robert Stern, Rem Koolhaas, Philippe Starck, David Rockwell Yabu Pushelberg to produce neighborhood-defining projects, establishing Related’s developments as integral components of Miami’s evolving cityscape. Pérez infuses each development with carefully curated collections, featuring pieces from master artists such as Frank Stella, Joan Mitchell, Willem de Kooning, Jim Dine and many others. 

Through the Related Philanthropic Foundation and The Jorge M. Pérez Family Foundation, Pérez has contributed more than $300 million to initiatives supporting education, economic development, health and well-being, the environment, and arts and culture. A signatory of The Giving Pledge, he remains committed to using philanthropy to build more equitable, vibrant communities.

To lead the conversation, Pérez will be joined by José Carlos Diaz, a specialist in modern and contemporary art with extensive experience in exhibition making, programming, and public art projects. He is the Senior Director of Curatorial Affairs & Chief Curator at the Pérez Art Museum Miami.

event_title: Can AI Reason Through Zoning? How AI Navigates Complex Rules
combined_title: Can AI Reason Through Zoning? How AI Navigates Complex Rules: Xiaofan Liang
description:
Abstract:

Zoning codes shape what can be built and where, yet their information remains buried in thousands of locally written documents that are difficult to search, compare, and analyze at scale. Zoning regulations present four particular challenges: they are heterogeneous, as jurisdictions organize and express similar rules differently; interdependent, as provisions interact through definitions, exceptions, overlays, and cross-references; multimodal, as requirements appear in text, tables, maps, and diagrams; and partly judgment-dependent, as some provisions require human interpretation and discretion. This talk presents a work-in-progress project that develops an agentic AI approach to transform zoning documents into structured, traceable regulatory data. Drawing on applications across more than 1,100 Michigan zoning documents and preliminary evaluations against human-coded data, I will discuss what AI can and cannot reliably interpret, where errors arise, and what these challenges reveal about the limits of computational reasoning over zoning regulations. The talk concludes by exploring a broader vision of computational zoning: making land-use regulations more accessible, interpretable, and comparable, and ultimately supporting inquiries across planning intentions, zoning rules, development scenarios, and community outcomes.
